content.p1: SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) was designed by the NSA and published by NIST in 1995. It produces a 160-bit (40-character hex) hash value. SHA-1 was the most widely used hash function for nearly two decades, securing SSL/TLS connections, digital certificates, and version control systems. While deprecated for security since 2017, SHA-1 remains deeply embedded in systems like Git where it serves as a content identifier.
content.what_desc: SHA-1 processes data in 512-bit blocks through 80 rounds of operations, producing a 160-bit message digest. It was designed to be computationally infeasible to find two different messages with the same hash (collision resistance) or to reconstruct the original message from its hash (preimage resistance). Google demonstrated the first practical collision attack (SHAttered) in 2017.

content.warning_desc: SHA-1 is deprecated for cryptographic security. Google's SHAttered attack proved practical collisions in 2017. All major browsers and CA/Browser Forum have stopped accepting SHA-1 certificates. Use SHA-256 or SHA-512 for new applications. Note: HMAC-SHA1 remains secure due to the HMAC construction.

faq.q1: Is SHA-1 still safe to use?
faq.a1: Not for security purposes. SHA-1 collisions have been demonstrated. However, it's still fine for non-security uses like Git commits or non-cryptographic checksums.
faq.q2: Why does Git still use SHA-1?
faq.a2: Git uses SHA-1 as a content identifier, not for security. Git is transitioning to SHA-256, but SHA-1 remains the default for backward compatibility.
faq.q3: What should I use instead of SHA-1?
faq.a3: Use SHA-256 for general purposes or SHA-512 for maximum security. For password hashing, use bcrypt or Argon2 instead of any SHA variant.
